source_text: Plane impensius respondebo ad excusationes huiusmodi artificum, quos numquam in domum dei admitti oportet si quis eam disciplinam norit. iam illa obici solita uox, non habeo aliud quo uiuam, districtius repercuti potest: uiuere ergo habes? quid tibi cum deo est, si tuis legibus uiuis? tum quod et de scripturis audent argumentari, dixisse apostolum: ut quisque fuerit inuentus, ita perseueret, possumus igitur omnes in peccatis perseuerare ex ista interpretatione. nec enim quisquam nostrum non peccator inuentus est, cum Christus non alia ex causa descenderit quam peccatorum liberandorum. item eundem praecepisse dicunt secundum suum exemplum, uti manibus suis unusquisque operetur ad uictum. si hoc: praeceptum ab omnibus manibus defenditur, credo et fures balneares manibus suis uiuere et ipsos latrones manibus agere quo uiuant, item falsarios utique non pedibus, sed manibus operari malas litteras, histriones uero non manibus solis, sed totis membris uictum elaborare. pateat igitur ecclesia omnibus, qui manibus et suo opere tolerant, si nulla exceptio est artium quas dei disciplina non recipit. sed ait quidam aduersus similitudinis interdictae propositionem: cur ergo Moses in eremo simulacrum serpentis ex aere fecit? seorsum figurae, quae dispositioni alicui arcanae praestruebantur, non ad erogationem legis, sed ad exemplarium causae suae. alioquin si haec ut aduersarii legis interpretemur, numquid et nos, quod et Marcionitae, inconstantiam adscribimus omnipotenti, quem illi hoc modo destruunt ut mutabilem, dum alibi uetat, alibi mandat? si quis autem dissimulat illam effigiem aerei serpentis suspenis in modum figuram designasse dominicae crucis a sepentibus id est ab angelis diaboli liberaturae nos, dum per semetipsam diabolum id est serpentem interfectum suspendit, siue quae alia figurae istius expositio dignioribus reuelata est, dummodo. apostolus affirmet omnia tunc figurate populo accidisse. bene, quod idem deus et lege uetuit similitudinem fieri et extraordinario praecepto serpentis similitudinem indixit. si eundem deum obseruas, habes legem eius, ne feceris similitudinem. si et praeceptum factae postea similitudinis respicis, et tu imitare Moysen, ne facias aduersus legem simulacrum aliquod, nisi et tibi deus iusserit.
orientation: Tertullian is answering excuses made by craftsmen who make idols, arguing that no one who knows Christian discipline may be admitted to God's house if they practice such arts.
pass_a_gloss: Plainly I will answer more vigorously to the excuses of craftsmen of this kind, whom it is never right to admit into the house of God if anyone knows that discipline. Now that voice which is usually thrown out, I have nothing else by which I may live, can be struck back more sharply: do you have to live then? What have you to do with God, if you live by your own laws? Then also they dare to argue from the scriptures, that the apostle said: as each one has been found, so let him continue; therefore we can all continue in sins by that interpretation. For not one of us has not been found a sinner, since Christ descended for no other cause than to set sinners free. Likewise they say that the same apostle commanded according to his own example, that each one should work with his own hands for a living. If this precept is defended by all hands, I believe that bath thieves also live by their own hands and that robbers themselves work with their hands so that they may live, likewise forgers certainly work bad letters not with their feet but with their hands, and actors indeed work out a living not with their hands only but with all their limbs. Let the church then be open to all who are supported by their hands and their own work, if there is no exception of arts which the discipline of God does not receive. But someone says against the proposition of the forbidden likeness: why then did Moses in the desert make a statue of a serpent from bronze? Figures are separate, which were being built up beforehand for some hidden arrangement, not for the carrying out of the law, but for the pattern of their own cause. Otherwise if we interpret these things as adversaries of the law, do we also, as the Marcionites do, ascribe inconsistency to the Almighty, whom they destroy in this way as changeable, while in one place he forbids, in another he commands? But if anyone pretends not to know that that image of the bronze serpent hung up in the manner of a figure designated the Lord's cross, which would free us from serpents, that is from the angels of the devil, while through itself it hung up the devil, that is the serpent, killed, or if any other explanation of that figure has been revealed to more worthy persons, provided that the apostle affirms that all things then happened figuratively to the people. Well, that the same God both forbade by law a likeness to be made and by an extraordinary command ordered the likeness of a serpent. If you observe the same God, you have his law: you shall not make a likeness. If you also look back at the command of the likeness made afterwards, you too imitate Moses, do not make any statue against the law, unless God has also commanded you.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'craftsmen' for artifices, not 'artisans' or 'makers'.
The glossary requires 'statue' for simulacrum, not 'image'.
The glossary requires 'discipline' for disciplina, not 'Christian teaching' or 'rule of faith'.

choices.english: do you have to live then
choices.why: Keeps the sharp rhetorical question and the force of 'habes' as obligation.
Preserves the technical term 'figura' used for typological prefigurations, matching the later 'figurate'.
Keeps the contrast with the standing law and the sense of a special, one-off order.

pass_b_english: I will answer the excuses of such craftsmen far more vigorously. If anyone knows that discipline, they should never be admitted into the house of God. The usual objection, "I have no other way to make a living," can be struck back more sharply: do you have to live, then? What do you have to do with God if you live by your own rules?

Then there is the argument they dare to draw from Scripture, that the apostle said each person should remain in the calling in which he was found (1 Corinthians 7:20). By that interpretation, all of us could continue in our sins. For none of us was found without sin, since Christ came down for no other reason than to set sinners free. They also say the same apostle commanded, following his own example, that each person should work with his own hands to earn a living (1 Thessalonians 4:11). If that command defends every kind of manual work, then I suppose pickpockets in the baths make their living with their hands, and robbers use their hands to do what they live by, and forgers certainly produce false documents not with their feet but with their hands, and actors earn their living not only with their hands but with their whole bodies. Let the church be open, then, to everyone who supports himself by his hands and his work, if no exception is made for the crafts that God's discipline does not accept.

But someone objects to the proposition that a likeness is forbidden: why, then, did Moses make a statue of a serpent out of bronze in the desert (Numbers 21:8-9)? Those figures were set apart. They were being prepared beforehand for a hidden purpose, not to relax the law, but to serve as patterns of their own meaning. Otherwise, if we interpret these things as opponents of the law do, should we too, like the Marcionites, attribute inconsistency to the Almighty? They destroy him in this way by making him changeable, since he forbids in one place and commands in another.

But if anyone fails to see that the figure of the bronze serpent hung up was designed to prefigure the Lord's cross, which would free us from serpents, that is, from the angels of the devil, while the serpent itself hung there as the devil slain, or whatever other explanation of that figure has been revealed to those more worthy, the apostle at least affirms that all these things happened to the people as figures (1 Corinthians 10:11). It is well that the same God both forbade the making of a likeness by the law and ordered the likeness of a serpent by an extraordinary command. If you obey the same God, you have his law: you shall not make a likeness (Exodus 20:4). But if you also look to the command for the likeness made afterward, then imitate Moses: do not make any statue contrary to the law, unless God has also commanded you.

problems.quote: he knows they should never be admitted into the house of God
problems.why: Latin is a conditional: 'if anyone knows that discipline'; English turns it into a declarative 'he knows'.
problems.fix: if anyone knows that discipline, they should never be admitted into the house of God.
problems.ruling: Latin conditional 'si quis eam disciplinam norit' vs English adds 'he knows' implying knowledge not in source

problems.quote: not to nullify the law but to serve as patterns of their own reality
problems.source_quote: non ad erogationem legis, sed ad exemplarium causae suae
problems.why: 'ad erogationem legis' means 'for dispensation of the law', not 'to nullify the law'; 'causae suae' = 'of their own case/cause'.
problems.fix: not for dispensation of the law, but as patterns of their own cause.
problems.ruling: Latin 'non ad erogationem legis' ≠ 'not to nullify the law'; 'exemplarium causae suae' ≠ 'patterns of their own reality'

problems.quote: which would free us from serpents—that is, from the angels of the devil—while it hung up the devil himself, the serpent, slain through his own instrument
problems.source_quote: a serpentibus id est ab angelis diaboli liberaturae nos, dum per semetipsam diabolum id est serpentem interfectum suspendit
problems.why: 'liberaturae nos' is future active participle: the cross will free us; 'per semetipsam' = 'by itself', not 'through his own instrument'; 'suspendit' = 'hung up', not 'slain'.
problems.fix: which would free us from serpents—that is, from the angels of the devil—while by itself it hung up the devil, that is, the serpent, slain.
problems.ruling: Latin says devil hangs the serpent; English says cross hangs devil and adds 'slain through his own instrument'

problems.why: 'Dummodo' introduces a conditional clause: 'provided that the apostle affirms'; the English drops the conditional force.
problems.fix: provided that the apostle affirms that all these things happened to the people as figures.
problems.ruling: Latin 'dummodo apostolus affirmet' is conditional; English drops conditional, changes meaning

fixed: Conditional restored: 'si quis eam disciplinam norit' = 'if anyone knows that discipline'.
Corrected 'ad erogationem legis' to 'for dispensation of the law' and 'causae suae' to 'of their own cause'.
Corrected 'per semetipsam' to 'by itself' and removed 'through his own instrument'; 'suspendit' = 'hung up', not 'slain'.
Restored conditional force of 'dummodo' as 'provided that'.

problems.quote: provided that the apostle affirms that all these things happened to the people as figures
problems.why: Sentence structure is broken: 'But if anyone fails to see that... provided that the apostle affirms...' does not parse.
problems.fix: Restructure: 'But if anyone fails to see this, the apostle affirms that all these things happened as figures.'

edits.old: But if anyone fails to see that the figure of the bronze serpent hung up was designed to prefigure the Lord's cross, which would free us from serpents—that is, from the angels of the devil—while by itself it hung up the devil, that is, the serpent, slain, or whatever other explanation of that figure has been revealed to those more worthy, provided that the apostle affirms that all these things happened to the people as figures (1 Corinthians 10:11).
edits.new: But if anyone fails to see that the figure of the bronze serpent hung up was designed to prefigure the Lord's cross, which would free us from serpents—that is, from the angels of the devil—while by itself it hung up the devil, that is, the serpent, slain, or whatever other explanation of that figure has been revealed to those more worthy, the apostle at least affirms that all these things happened to the people as figures (1 Corinthians 10:11).

fixed: The sentence structure was broken because 'provided that' made the final clause conditional on the preceding 'if anyone fails to see' clause, leaving the sentence without a main clause. The source has 'dummodo. apostolus affirmet' — 'provided that the apostle affirms' — but in the English the whole passage is one long sentence where 'provided that' does not work grammatically. Changing to 'the apostle at least affirms' restores a main clause while keeping the sense that the apostle's affirmation stands regardless of which explanation is accepted.

last_rejected.why: The source has a conditional 'si quis dissimulat' ('if anyone fails to see') that governs the whole long sentence, but the English drops the main clause consequence, leaving a fragment.
last_rejected.fix: But if anyone fails to see that the figure of the bronze serpent hung up prefigured the Lord's cross, which would free us from serpents—that is, from the angels of the devil—while by itself it hung up the devil, that is, the serpent, slain, or whatever other explanation of that figure has been revealed to those more worthy—provided that the apostle affirms that all these things happened to the people as figures (1 Corinthians 10:11)—then let him note this.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin conditional 'si quis ... dissimulat ... dummodo apostolus affirmet' is rendered as English conditional 'But if anyone fails to see ... provided that the apostle affirms', followed by consequent 'It is well that...'

polish.changed: Clarified the broken sentence about the bronze serpent by restructuring it so the apostle's affirmation stands as the main clause, and added a brief explanation of the Marcionites as a sect that accused God of inconsistency.

notes.fix: Note: 'Marcionites = sect that rejected the Old Testament God as inconsistent.'

notes.why: 'Dispensation of the law' and 'patterns of their own cause' are opaque; the sentence does not make sense as English.

notes.quote: while by itself it hung up the devil, that is, the serpent, slain
notes.why: The syntax is tangled; it is unclear what 'by itself' refers to and how the serpent/devil is 'hung up... slain.'
notes.fix: Rewrite: 'the bronze serpent prefigured the cross, which defeated the devil, represented by the serpent.'
